title: Why Peak FLOPS is the Wrong Yardstick for Inference Hardware
gist: Lauro Rizzatti (a VSORA investor) argues peak FLOPS is the wrong metric for AI inference hardware: decode is memory-bandwidth and KV-cache-capacity bound (roughly 1 FLOP/byte vs. a GPU's ~300 FLOP/byte balance point), long contexts blow past HBM capacity, and chips should be judged on TTFT, inter-token latency, goodput, energy per token and cost per request; VSORA's cacheless Jotunn8 is cited as one response.

insights.claim: Inference is not a lighter version of training but a different workload, so ranking AI processors by peak FLOPS made sense for training but much less for inference-dominated economics.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Hardware winners in the inference era may differ from training-era GPU leaders.
insights.quote: inference is not a lighter version of training. It is a different job altogether.
insights.locator: For a decade we have ranked

insights.claim: Training is bound by compute and, at scale, by interconnect communication; prefill is compute-bound and measured by time to first token; low-batch decode is bound by memory bandwidth and KV-cache capacity and measured by inter-token latency and goodput.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Map each AI workload to its bottleneck resource when valuing chip, memory and networking suppliers.

insights.claim: Training memory must hold weights plus activations, gradients and optimizer state, together several times model size, and thousands of chips must exchange gradients each step, so interconnect sets the pace at scale.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti

insights.claim: In chatbots, coding assistants and especially agents that plan and call tools, most inference time is spent in decode rather than prefill.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Agentic AI growth shifts demand toward memory-bandwidth-optimized hardware.

insights.claim: A popular data-center GPU with about 1 petaFLOPS dense FP16 and 3.35 TB/s from five HBM3 stacks needs roughly 300 operations per byte fetched to stay busy, whereas batch-1 decode delivers about one FLOP per byte.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: GPUs run far below peak in low-batch decode; utilisation gap is the opening for inference-specific silicon.

insights.claim: Batching amortises weight fetches across users, but each user's KV cache is read separately, so long contexts pull utilisation back down and bytes per second, not TFLOPS, set decode throughput.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Memory bandwidth (HBM) is the binding constraint for inference throughput.
insights.quote: In decode, bytes per second, not rated TFLOPS, set the throughput.

insights.claim: For Llama 3.1 70B with an FP16 KV cache, the cache is about 320 KB per token, so one user at 128K context needs about 43 GB, four users 172 GB and eight users 344 GB, almost 2.5x the 141 GB of HBM on an H200.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Long-context agent workloads drive outsized demand for HBM capacity and tiered memory.

insights.claim: Decode reads the entire KV cache for every generated token, making the memory wall simultaneously a capacity problem and a bandwidth problem.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Both HBM capacity and bandwidth scale with context length; bullish memory suppliers.
insights.locator: And decode reads all of it

insights.claim: Industry responses to the inference memory wall fall into three groups: locality (SRAM-heavy and wafer-scale designs), capacity (HBM and tiered SRAM-HBM-DDR hierarchies), and orchestration (compiler-directed dataflow and disaggregated prefill/decode).
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Use this taxonomy to classify inference chip startups and their trade-offs.

insights.claim: GPUs span all three inference strategies with unmatched software maturity but tend toward underutilisation in low-batch decode.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: GPU incumbency rests on software; the decode efficiency gap is its vulnerability.

insights.claim: VSORA's Jotunn8 inference processor removes the cache hierarchy and relies on the compiler to place every operand in a large register-file-style memory, with VSORA claiming over 50% sustained compute efficiency versus theoretical peak.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Claim needs validation on real serving workloads; note the author is a VSORA investor.
insights.quote: Caches are a bet on reuse and decode loses that bet on every token.
insights.locator: One example of a design built

insights.claim: None of this means GPUs are obsolete; every architecture should be judged against the actual job, and a faster arithmetic engine is not always a faster inference engine.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Avoid binary 'GPU vs. ASIC' framing; evaluate per workload.
insights.locator: None of this means GPUs are obsolete.

insights.claim: Inference benchmarks should disclose model version, precision, context length, input/output mix, concurrency and serving software, since changing any one can flip rankings.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Discount vendor inference claims lacking full workload disclosure.
insights.quote: Change any one and the ranking can flip.

insights.claim: Inference hardware should be judged on time to first token, inter-token latency, goodput within service targets, energy per token and cost per completed request rather than peak FLOPS.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Shift chip valuation toward delivered tokens per watt and per dollar.

insights.claim: In modern silicon, moving a byte costs far more energy than computing with it, so architectures that move less data per token should show lower energy per token.
insights.speaker: Lauro Rizzatti
insights.so_what: Data-movement-minimising designs have a structural energy-cost advantage in inference.
